judgement.summary: A single-concept plan ("signal from noise") that walks a vertical scroll from a particle-field hero through Helix, Rent Map, a deliberately mute Meridian strip, two honestly downsized projects, origins, education and contact, with per-section WebGL scenes, phone/reduced-motion/no-JS fallbacks and a build-needs list. Its greatest weakness is that the concept and visuals are generic to any data analyst — the page is still the usual website sections with a separate decorative scene in each, no single persistent object, and the one genuinely personal structure (the analysis memo) is confined to two case studies instead of shaping the page.

final.question: "Signal from noise." Every section opens on something scattered and unclear and ends on something resolved and legible

swap.reason: "Scattered data resolves into something legible" is the generic story of any data or product analyst and could sit unchanged on another analyst's site; only the section copy, not the concept, is particular to Rafael.

backdrop.reason: The plan itself says every scroll-scrubbed scene has "a static end-state image as its fallback" and the site must read fully without JavaScript, so deleting the 3D costs only decoration.

depth.reason: Each section replays the same noise-to-signal beat independently and the middle run (Meridian, AutoPilot, FraudShield, Origins) could be reordered without the plan changing, despite the hero/close bookend.

clipart.reason: There is no single central object — the scroll is a sequence of unrelated scenes (particle field, timeline curve, Lisbon map, merging nodes, scatter plot) — and the recurring drifting-points-into-a-grid motif is close to the stock emblem of data work.

honesty.reason: The final plan drops the 35%, holds the bank to LinkedIn-only text, rescopes FraudShield and AutoPilot, credits the hackathon team and the study group, and refuses the "genomics researcher" label.

thirty_seconds.reason: Hero carries the name, "Product Analyst, Lisbon" and the honest line; the fixed nav offers Contact and section jumps, and the first two case studies deliver verifiable proof (60%, ~3,000/month, live link) without reading the whole page.

plain_reader.reason: "I make dashboards people actually use" plus name and role is plain enough for an outsider and specific enough that a hiring product team would respect it.
